p: FDA asks how much potential a change has to have an adverse effect on the identity, strength, quality, purity or potency of the product, as these relate to its safety or effectiveness. Substantial potential makes a major change; moderate potential a moderate change; minimal potential a minor change.
The same three tests apply to NDAs and ANDAs (21 CFR 314.70, applied to ANDAs by 314.97) and to BLAs (21 CFR 601.12).
Prior approval supplement (PAS): major changes. Product made with the change is distributed only after FDA approves.
Supplement - Changes Being Effected in 30 Days (CBE-30): moderate changes. Distribution can start 30 days after FDA receives the supplement, unless FDA says otherwise in that time.
Supplement - Changes Being Effected (CBE-0): moderate changes FDA allows at once. Distribution can start when FDA receives the supplement.
Annual report (AR): minor changes. Make the change, then describe it in the next annual report, due within 60 days of the anniversary of approval.

sections.h: Do and tell, or tell and wait
p: The app shows a badge on every result: do and tell (annual report), tell then do at once (CBE-0), tell, wait 30 days, then do (CBE-30), or wait for approval (PAS). It is the first thing a change control board needs to know.

When related changes are filed together, use the most restrictive category of the individual changes (guidance section XII). Unrelated changes can go separately, so a minor change does not have to wait for a major one.

A move to a site that FDA has never inspected for the type of operation, or that restarts an operation stopped for more than two years, is a prior approval supplement (VI.B.1). So is a move to a site without a satisfactory CGMP inspection for that operation (VI.B.2).

Some products make a move major even to a good site: modified-release products, products whose primary packaging controls the dose (VI.B.3), aseptic processing into a new or dissimilar area (VI.B.4) and terminally sterilized products into a newly built facility at a different site (VI.B.5).
Otherwise a move is a CBE-30 (VI.C.1.a), with special cases for aseptic areas that already make similar products (VI.C.1.b), primary packaging (VI.C.1.c) and testing labs (VI.C.1.d).
Secondary packaging, labeling, ink imprinting and early intermediates are annual report items (VI.D).

A change of technology (wet to dry granulation, a new drying method, a new synthetic route) is a prior approval supplement (VII.B.4). So are changes that may affect controlled release (VII.B.1) or sterility assurance (VII.B.2).

Other changes to process, parameters or equipment are CBE-30 (VII.C.1.a). Equipment of the same design and operating principle, and changes in scale, are annual report items (VII.D.1) unless another rule applies.

The 2004 guidance keeps the SUPAC categories for components and composition. For immediate-release solids, SUPAC-IR Level 1 changes are annual report items; Levels 2 and 3 need prior approval, Level 3 usually with an in vivo bioequivalence study.

Tightening a limit is minor (VIII.D.3). Adding a test that increases assurance is a CBE-0 (VIII.C.2.a). Relaxing a limit or deleting a test needs prior approval (VIII.B.1, VIII.B.2), except where it follows a compendium (CBE-30, VIII.C.1.e) or concerns early raw materials (CBE-30, VIII.C.1.b).

A new regulatory procedure, or one that gives less assurance, needs prior approval (VIII.B.3, VIII.B.4). Other changes to a regulatory procedure are CBE-30. Alternative procedures with the same or greater assurance are annual report items (VIII.D.2).

sections.h: Most labeling changes need prior approval
p: 21 CFR 314.70(b)(2)(v) makes labeling changes prior approval supplements, except the safety and editorial changes the rule lists. New indications and population changes come as efficacy supplements with clinical data.

Adding or strengthening a contraindication, warning, precaution or adverse reaction, an instruction for safer use, or deleting misleading claims can go in at once as a CBE-0, when based on newly acquired information with reasonable evidence of a causal association (314.70(c)(6)(iii); 601.12(f)(2) for biologics).

If FDA becomes aware of new safety information that it believes should be in the labeling, it notifies the holder. The holder has 30 days to submit a supplement with the change or a statement of why it is not warranted; disagreements follow a set timetable, after which FDA can order the change.
ANDA labeling must be the same as the reference listed drug's, apart from permitted differences, so generic holders update their labeling when the brand's changes.

A comparability protocol (FDA's name for a post-approval change management protocol under ICH Q12) describes a future change, the studies and the acceptance criteria. It is approved first, in a prior approval supplement; afterwards the change it covers can be filed in the lower category it sets.

FDA's 2021 guidance for certain biological products treats many process, facility and specification changes as prior approval: new master cell banks, new purification steps or resins, viral clearance changes. The app shows when a result comes from guidance written for small molecules.

ICH Q12 lets a holder agree with FDA which elements are established conditions. Changes to other elements are managed in the quality system without a filing. The app adds established conditions and the product lifecycle management document in a later phase.

Changes to EU marketing authorisations are variations under Regulation (EC) No 1234/2008, amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/1701 (applying from 1 January 2025). The Commission's classification guidelines C/2025/5045 apply from 15 January 2026 and replace the 2013 guidelines.
Type IB and II variations follow the guidelines in force on the submission date; Type IA follow those in force on the implementation date.

Type IA: do and tell within 12 months, often in the annual update. Type IA-IN: do and tell immediately. Type IB: tell, wait 30 days without objection, then do. Type II: wait for approval. Extension: a new strength, form or route, assessed like a new application.

Some changes need no variation (for example a working cell bank under an approved protocol), and some use a different procedure (a transfer, or an Article 61(3) notification for labelling that does not touch the SmPC).

Most Type IA and IA-IN entries list numbered conditions. Every one must be met; if one is not, the change is Type IB by default, unless the guidelines name Type II. The app shows the conditions as a checklist and answers the product ones (sterile, biological, dosage form) from the product profile.

lessons.title: EU quality changes that come up most

p: A new site for a manufacturing operation on the finished product is Type IB (Q.II.b.1(e)); Type II when the site needs an initial or product-specific inspection, or the process is novel or complex. Packaging sites can be Type IA-IN when the conditions are met; immediate packaging only for non-sterile products.

Up to ten times (up or down) for immediate-release oral forms and non-sterile solutions can be Type IA (Q.II.b.4); beyond ten times Type IB; biologics needing comparability Type II. Minor process changes can be Type IA when all eight conditions of Q.II.b.3 are met.

Changes within the acceptance criteria and new non-impurity attributes can be Type IA; going outside the criteria is Type II. Shelf-life extensions with real-time data are Type IA-IN for immediate-release film-coated tablets and Type IB otherwise; storage changes for biologics are Type II.

lessons.title: Grouping, worksharing and timing in the EU

p: Several variations to one authorisation can be grouped when they are related: a case listed in Annex III, or agreed with the authority. The group follows its highest type. EMA's Q&A lists groupings that are generally not accepted, such as quality with clinical changes or active substance with finished product changes, unless justified.

Unrelated Type IA changes to one authorisation can be notified together in the annual update. The same Type IB, II or group for several authorisations of one holder can be assessed once through worksharing (Article 20); the same Type IA or IA-IN for several authorisations can be super-grouped (Article 7a).

Type IB is accepted 30 days after a valid notification without objection. Type II runs a 60-day evaluation (90 for indications, 30 for some safety changes) plus clock stops. Quality-only Type II changes can be implemented after a positive opinion; changes to the product information wait for the amended decision.

For biological products, CDSCO's guidance PAC/2024 (version 1.2, implemented 16 May 2024) sorts quality, safety and efficacy changes into four levels: Level I supplement and Level II notifiable change need approval before commercial use; Level III is an annual notification in the first quarter; Level IV is a record kept under GMP.
For chemical new drugs there is no codified classification in force: CDSCO decides case by case on a post-approval change application through SUGAM.

Under rule 2(w)(ii) of the NDCT Rules, a drug with new or modified claims, such as a new indication, dosage, dosage form or route, is a new drug again and needs a new permission (Form CT-18 to import, CT-21 to manufacture). CDSCO decides within 90 working days.

The draft G.S.R. 97(E) of 2 February 2026 would add Level I, II and III for quality changes to new drugs, defined by substantial, moderate and minimal potential to affect quality, the same three tests FDA uses. Levels I and II would need prior approval; Level III would go in an annual submission in the first quarter, except shelf-life changes. A draft of 9 March 2026 would extend this to licences under the Drugs Rules, 1945. The app shows the draft as a what-if.

lessons.title: One core data sheet, many labels

p: Companies keep a company core data sheet (CCDS) with the core safety information. When it changes, every regional label must follow: the US prescribing information, the EU SmPC and package leaflet, the Indian prescribing information and others.

A new adverse reaction based on new information is a CBE-0 supplement in the US, a Type II variation in the EU unless it implements wording the authorities already agreed (then Type IA-IN), and in India a Level I or II change for biologicals or a case-by-case application for chemical drugs.
The Labelling page tracks one CCDS change across regions: where it goes in each label, its category, the company's target date and how far each region lags.

Health Canada sorts changes after the Notice of Compliance (NOC) into four levels. Level I is a supplement (an SNDS, or SANDS for a generic): implement only after a new NOC. Level II has two kinds: a supplement for safety labelling, and a notifiable change for biologics, implemented after a No Objection Letter. Level III is a notice of change: implement, then tell Health Canada. Level IV is a record kept under GMP.
For pharmaceuticals there is no notifiable change: the 2019 revision of the quality guidance moved those changes to Level I or Level III.

Appendix 1 of the quality guidance lists each change with conditions. When every condition for Level III is met the change is a notice; if one is not met, it moves up to the next level. A series of small changes can together justify a higher level.

Pharmaceutical Level III changes are best filed at implementation; biologics file them within 12 months. Biologics also have an immediate notification, from 21 days before to 14 days after implementation, mostly through an approved protocol.

Health Canada starts with protocols (PACMPs) for biologic and radiopharmaceutical products: submissions are accepted after a 90-day period that began on 13 August 2026. Established conditions are not implemented yet, and pharmaceutical protocols follow later.

lessons.title: Switzerland: the EU list, Swiss clocks

p: Since 1 February 2026 Swissmedic classifies variations with a revised list in Annex 7 of the TPLRO, harmonised as far as possible with the EU list. The codes (for example Q.II.b.1) and most conditions are the same, so an EU classification is a good start.
Swiss-only variations are numbered from 100, and the variation form valid from 1 February 2026 must be used.

Type IA-IN is notified within one month after implementation, not immediately. Type IB is accepted if Swissmedic does not object within 70 days (10 days formal control and 60 days evaluation). Type II has time limits up to 270 days of Swissmedic time, plus the applicant's time to answer.

There is no EU worksharing, and the holder must be established in Switzerland. Several variations for one product form a multiple application, processed on the longest time limit; safety-related variations cannot be part of one.

Japan does not classify changes from a list. The approval form, with its approved matters, is legally binding. Changing an approved matter needs a partial change approval. Items the form marks as minor change items are notified within 30 days after the change. Items outside the form need no filing.

Article 47 of the Enforcement Regulations keeps some changes out of the minor route whatever the form says: changes that affect the nature or safety of the product, deleting or changing specifications, pathogen inactivation, and dosage or indications.

A site change with an unchanged method can go through a rapid partial change review (about 3 months). Since 2024 a trial lets designated moderate change items use a short review, and since 2025 another trial lets designated low-impact items be reported once a year.
Change plans (Japan's PACMP) have two steps: confirm the plan, then notify each change made under it. The change becomes an approved matter 40 working days after acceptance (20 in special cases).

Variations to prequalified finished products follow WHO TRS 981 Annex 3. An annual notification is made within 12 months of implementation. An immediate notification is made as the change is implemented. A minor variation can be implemented if WHO has not started correspondence within 60 days of acknowledging it. A major variation needs WHO's letter of acceptance first.
Some changes, such as a new strength, dosage form or route, need a new application.

The timeline table published by PQT prevails over the guideline. A change that is not listed is major by default, unless it is justified as an unclassified minor variation (suffix u) or agreed with PQT in advance.

A new manufacturing site is minor only if WHO or a stringent authority inspected it in the last three years. Adding nitrosamine controls is an immediate notification. Grouping is allowed for consequential changes, the same change to several products, or annual notifications.

lessons.title: Established conditions, PACMPs and the PLCM document

p: ICH Q12 splits the quality dossier into established conditions (ECs), which are legally binding, and supportive information. Only a change to an EC needs a regulatory submission; everything else is managed in the quality system.

Each EC gets a reporting category by risk: prior approval for high risk, a moderate notification for medium risk and a low notification for low risk. Better process knowledge (an enhanced or performance-based approach) can mean fewer ECs or lower categories.
A post-approval change management protocol (PACMP) agrees a change in advance in two steps: the plan with its studies and acceptance criteria, then the change itself, reported in a lower category.

The product lifecycle management (PLCM) document lists the ECs with their categories, the protocols and the post-approval CMC commitments. The Lifecycle page builds all three for a fictional product and maps each category to the US, EU, Swiss and Japanese routes.

lessons.title: Comparability after a biologic process change (ICH Q5E)

p: After a manufacturing change to a biological product, the holder shows that the product before and after is highly similar, and that any difference has no adverse impact on safety or efficacy. The products need not be identical.

The exercise compares physicochemical properties, biological activity, purity and impurities, and stability, guided by a risk assessment of what the change could affect. Accelerated and stress studies often show subtle differences that release tests miss.

sections.h: When quality data are not enough
p: If quality data cannot rule out an impact (for example a changed glycosylation profile that could affect exposure), nonclinical or clinical bridging studies may be needed.
In the classifier, changes that need a comparability assessment are classified more strictly; in the EU a batch size change for a biological substance that needs one is Type II (Q.I.a.3(c)).
